column2: Joab knows the king's heart is on Absalom; on remains open rather than a supplied longing or hostility.
Joab recruits a wise Tekoa woman, directs mourning dress and no oil, and tells her to resemble a long-term mourner.
The royal approach and prescribed speech lead into the explicit narrator statement that Joab put the words in her mouth.
Entry, falling, bowing and doubled Help retain the appeal's sequence and repetition; the king is addressed as a human.
The king asks what troubles her and she claims widowhood and a dead husband; this remains her staged account, not verified personal history.
Two sons fight with no intermediary, and one kills his brother; no previous motive or identification is supplied.

Propose Behold instead of Now and They will extinguish instead of They would extinguish, preserving the presentative and future in the claimed threat. Family demand, heir, remaining ember and loss of name remain.
column3: The future belongs to her account and does not establish that the family or threat exists outside the staged story.

column2: Go in good health retains the selected reassurance alongside the promised orders concerning her.
The woman assigns lawlessness to herself and her father's house while declaring king and throne innocent; no added criminal judgment is implied by the narrator.
The king asks who speaks to her, commands bringing him and says he will not touch him again.
column3: The second him is the selected masculine pronoun and its antecedent remains unresolved; you is not substituted to smooth the account.

column2: The positive blood-avenger infinitive, emphatic nonremoval of her son and king's oath against a fallen hair remain.
column3: The infinitive's logical relation to remembering the Lord is unresolved. No lest, restrain or negative absent from that clause is inserted; the final oath's conditional form is rendered as emphatic negation.

column2: The servant seeks permission to speak a word, and the king gives it; courtly self-reference remains ordinary human address.
The accusation concerning God's people and the king's failure to restore his banished one remain.
column3: The inherited negative rhetorical question interprets the initial particle and verbless comparison; there is no separate Greek not governing offence. An affirmative statement or differently shaped question remains possible.

column2: Propose For we must certainly die to preserve the explanatory hoti. Spilled ungatherable water and both positive divine actions remain.
column3: God will take a life and planning to banish are not rewritten with negatives from another witness. The participle's subject and relation to the finite clause remain open.

column2: Propose Now what I have come to say to preserve the discourse transition. People will see me and the servant's future speech remain.
column3: Let someone speak supplies a subject for the third-person imperative; the nested speech boundary and referent remain provisional rather than an accepted reconstruction.

column2: The king's hearing and deliverance concern the man seeking to remove mother and son from God's inheritance; the explanatory for remains.
Word as an offering, the God-angel comparison for hearing good and evil and future divine presence remain.
column3: Offering follows the selected sacrifice noun, not a substituted comfort term. The angel comparison does not convert the king into a divine addressee.

column2: The king requests concealment of nothing he asks, and the woman invites his speech; no answer to the forthcoming Joab question is supplied early.
Propose For your servant Joab to retain the causal explanation for her oath-bound agreement. Joab's command and placing all words in her mouth remain emphatic.
Turning the matter around interprets the face-of-the-matter idiom; the comparison of royal wisdom to God's angel and knowledge of everything in the land remain her praise.
Propose Behold, I have now acted to retain the presentative before the king's assent and command to bring back young Absalom.
Joab falls, bows, blesses and recognizes favour because the king granted the request; first-person I within third-person servant language remains.
Joab personally goes to Geshur and brings Absalom to Jerusalem, preserving the two named endpoints.
Return to his own house is paired with prohibited access to the king's face, and both directions are fulfilled.
Absalom's exceptional praise and lack of blemish from foot sole to head remain without a separate statement of moral perfection.
Periodic cutting because of heaviness and two hundred royal shekels remain.
column3: From days to days is not fixed to a yearly schedule here, nor is the weight converted or corrected to fit an assumed plausible haircut.

column2: Three sons, daughter Tamar, her beauty and the full Rehoboam-wife/Abijah-birth notice remain.
column3: The genealogical relationships are not harmonized with other biblical accounts or used to merge this Tamar with Absalom's sister.

column2: Two full Jerusalem years without seeing the king's face remain distinct from the earlier Geshur stay.
Two summonses and Joab's two refusals remain, with him explicitly clarified as Joab in inherited English.
The neighbouring barley plot, arson order and burning remain, including the full report by Joab's servants in torn garments.
column3: Burned the barley resolves the feminine plural object to the barley plants; the plot remains the location rather than a different crop.

column2: Joab comes to Absalom's house and questions why his servants burned the plot; no retaliatory action is invented.
Propose Behold at the initial I sent to you, retaining both presentatives in Absalom's explanation. Geshur, still being there, not seeing the king's face and conditional death request remain.
column3: The negative I have not seen is the selected reading, not a wish to see. Nested speech boundaries and the ultimate addressee of put me to death remain provisional.

column2: Joab reports, the king summons Absalom, Absalom bows and falls before him, and the king kisses him warmly.
column3: The supplied king as summoning subject is inferred from the scene; the Greek does not separately name the caller in that clause.
